title: London Theatre News & Reviews Roundups
transcript: Now last week saw two revivals tickle the critics' funny bones, plus a play about Marilyn Monroe that got the worst reviews of the year. First, Abigail's Party. Now Alison Steadman is forever associated with the part of Beverly, but all the critics agreed that Tamzin Outhwaite made it her own. "Flinty, ferocious, and quite fabulous." Said the Financial Times. The critics were not so unified about the quality of Nadia Fall's production and whether Mike Leigh's 1980s play had dated. Although most felt it worked well. "Fall's deft direction maximizes the comedy, but also the agonizing and almost unbearable sadness lurking below." Said Broadway World. Now the worst reviews of the year, worse even than those for Trainspotting, greeted Charlene Cooper Cohen's play Who Killed Marilyn, which is about the life and death of Marilyn Monroe. Pixie Lott as the iconic movie star emerged with a few kind words, but not many. But the play, directed by Philip William McKinley, was "Like a Wikipedia entry." Said the Mail What's on Stage and Broadway World. The average rating of 1.4 will take a lot of beating. There's never a long gap between productions of Shakespeare's much loved comedy As You Like It. In fact, there's one coming up at Stratford soon. But here I'm talking about the one at the Globe. While the critics enjoyed Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine's comical approach to their version, "Rumbustious fun." Said the Telegraph. Is that a word anybody uses in normal conversation? And they praised many of the actors, including Lola Shalam's Rosalind, Johnny Broadbent's Touchstone, and Katherine Pierce's Jaques. "Shalam dazzles nearly everyone else off the stage." Said The Stage. In theater news, the National Theatre's production of Pride, uh, a musical based on the film, which is currently sold out at the Dorfman Theatre, will transfer to the Bridge Theatre. It'll be the first presentation by the new owners, the Trafalgar Group. And BBC Radio 4 will air a series of audio dramas adapted from Royal Court Theatre plays to mark the venue's 70th anniversary. It'll begin with a newly commissioned, uh, radio version of Lucy Kirkwood's The Children. Uh, that's on the 26th of September. Then seven more radio adaptations from the BBC's archives will be broadcast on Radio 4 Extra. These include John Osborne's Look Back in Anger, Arnold Wesker's Roots, Sizwe Banzi is Dead, Caryl Churchill's Top Girls, Timberlake Wertenbaker's Our Country's Good, Debbie Tucker Green's Random, and Charlene James' Cutting It. The season is curated by playwright Mark Ravenhill, and I'm sure they'll all be available on BBC Sounds. I'm Paul Seven Lewis, and please check out my reviews of London shows on my YouTube channel, Theater Reviews with Paul Seven, and on my website, theater.reviews. See you soon. >>
classificationReason: London theatre news roundup summarizing other critics' reviews across multiple productions (Abigail's Party, Who Killed Marilyn, etc.). No single show focus and no first-hand attendance.
